claim: In Testing mode Google caps you at 100 test users, and authorizations and refresh tokens expire after 7 days.
origin: Our own planning notes, before any source was read
what: The first pages we fetched said only that a user cap applies and that refresh token lifetime is limited, with no numbers, so we could not verify either figure. A later fetch of Google's "Manage app audience" page states both.
quote: Authorizations by a test user will expire seven days from the time of consent.

claim: How long does sensitive-scope verification take?
what: One page says up to 10 days. Another says it might take several months, depending on the data's sensitivity. We did not pick one: the guide shows both and labels the claim as conflicting.
quote: The sensitive scope verification process can take up to 10 days to complete.

claim: Apps using sensitive scopes need 1 to 3 days for Google review.
origin: A plain, single-prompt answer from the same model
what: Contradicted by the official page. Hand-reviewed.
quote: The sensitive scope verification process can take up to 10 days to complete.

claim: Slack App Review for public distribution takes 3 to 7 business days.
origin: A plain, single-prompt answer from the same model
what: Contradicted: the preliminary review alone can take up to 10 business days, and a functional review of up to 10 weeks follows. This understates the wait by an order of magnitude. Hand-reviewed.
quote: Currently, the preliminary part of the review takes up to 10 business days to receive feedback, while the functional review takes up to 10 weeks for new submissions and 6 weeks for published apps resubmitting changes.

claim: GitHub's callback URL rules are just "up to 10 callback URLs".
origin: A first research pass, which only read the creation page
what: The authorizing-apps page describes more: wildcard matching is now configurable per callback URL, apps created before August 3, 2026 have it switched on, and loopback URLs may use any port. Reading one more page changed the advice.
quote: Apps that had a single callback URL enabled prior to August 3, 2026 have wildcard matching enabled for that callback URL.

claim: GitHub's creation guide says to type your callback into a field called "Authorization callback URL".
origin: GitHub's own docs, compared with the live form during our real setup attempt
what: The live form says "Redirect URI", offers a per-URI wildcard checkbox, and the guide does not mention either. The redirect behavior itself matched the docs when we tested it: exact match enforced, any loopback port accepted. The guide now flags the mismatch so a developer is not thrown by it.
quote: The registration form labels the field "Redirect URI", with the button "Add redirect URI", not "Authorization callback URL".

claim: Google enforces HTTPS redirect URIs when you create an OAuth client.
origin: A common assumption, and what the docs imply
what: In our real attempt, Google created a client with a plain http redirect URI on a non-localhost host without any error. The restriction only appeared afterwards: publishing to production was blocked, and some scopes were hidden, until the URI was removed. Localhost over http is exempt. A developer who builds on http only finds out at the end.
quote: We entered http://example.com/cb as the redirect URI and clicked Create. Google created the client with no error.

claim: An agent can complete the Google consent-screen setup on its own once you are signed in.
origin: Our own expectation before the attempt
what: Nearly all of it, yes, but not the last step: the wizard requires agreeing to Google's API services user data policy, which only the account owner can accept. The agent stopped and asked. The client secret is also shown only once, so someone has to capture it at creation.
quote: Accepting the Google API services user data policy needs the account owner's explicit agreement.

claim: The automatic draft said Slack apps are "web dashboard only" and left the verdict unknown.
what: The curated guide found what the draft missed: apps can be created through an API from a manifest, with one human step to generate the first token. This is why seeds are curated by hand and live guides are labeled as not human-verified.
quote: is used to create apps from JSON manifests.

claim: A live guide gave X the verdict "works immediately; review only to be listed".
what: The quote it cited was real and on the page, so the existence check passed, but it said nothing about review or listing. The support check caught it and reset the verdict to unknown. This is why every claim gets two checks, not one.
quote: Some endpoints require user-context authentication (OAuth 1.0a or 2.0)

claim: A live guide labeled Notion "creatable through an API".
what: The label was inferred from an unrelated verified item about webhooks. The setup method now needs its own supporting quote, otherwise it shows as not stated.

claim: "No approval needed" is backed by the quote "Click Register application."
what: No quote can prove that something is absent. The second review flagged it. These verdicts are now labeled as inferred from what the official pages do not mention, and are only allowed when at least two official pages were read.

claim: gemini-2.5-flash is a safe default model.
what: It appears in the model list but returns "no longer available to new users". A probe also showed no model offers search grounding on this tier, and one model hung for 44 seconds before failing. The app now tries several models in order, with a deadline and a cooldown for any that just failed.

claim: Correct English quotes verify against Google's pages.
what: One Google page came back in German, so English quotes could never match. The fetcher now asks for English. Separately, GitHub's markdown embeds SVG icons inside sentences, which also broke correct quotes. The matcher now sees through links and inline HTML.

claim: A keyword score is enough to find the OAuth page from a docs landing page.
what: Typeform's page lives at get-started/applications, which scored zero. The model now chooses which links to follow, reading the anchor text, and keywords remain only as a fallback. After the change, Typeform went from nothing found to 12 of 12 claims backed by quotes.

claim: LinkedIn's OAuth overview and its access guide agree on which permissions are open.
what: The overview page still gives older scope names as examples. The guide notes this so developers check the current list.
quote: Open permissions available to all applications are of this type such as `r_liteprofile`, `r_emailaddress`, and `w_member_social`.
